messages.subject: Advice on planting
messages.text:
Hello I live on 40 acress on Madeline Island in Lake Superior. 
 We plant for humming birds which love our gardens. My current gardens are raised beds. I have a 120ft of currently. 
 Our soil is red clay, sand, dirt. We bring in a couple truckloads 
 every year. I would use the good soil for planting.
 We tried a few years ago, collected 
 Seeds, planted in ground in fall and unfortunately nothing. Milkweed does grow here. Just not how I planted. Would like to do a raised bed just for milkeeed. We had hundreds of bees and butterflies 🦋 over the years, now sadly not so many. 
 Want to start seeds inside. Do not have much refrigerator space to help.sprout.
 Can you help please! I read the directions on your site but wondering if I can easily grow a few hundred plants
 And transplant as soon as weather. Permits.
 I can be reached at 715 209 1161 or
 lucamartin2010@gmail.com. 
 Thank you so much! Hope you can help me to help our beautiful 🦋 
 Joan Martin lucamartin2010@gmail.com

messages.subject: Re: Advice on planting
messages.text:
Hi Joan,

Sorry for the long delay getting back to you, spring is our most intense stretch and this one took far too long to reach you.

Your setup sounds like a great fit for milkweed. A raised bed with good imported soil is actually ideal, especially since your native red clay can be tough for germination. Here's what I'd recommend for starting a few hundred plants indoors:

Since you don't have much fridge space, the good news is that you can cold-stratify seeds without taking up much room at all. Just place the seeds between two damp paper towels, seal them in a small zip-lock bag, and tuck them in whatever fridge space you can spare, even a small corner works. Thirty days is the minimum; sixty is better and really increases germination rates. After stratification, plant them in seed trays or small cells, cover lightly (no more than 5mm of soil), keep moist, and place under a clear plastic cover or near a sunny window to create a greenhouse effect. They should start sprouting within a few weeks.

For transplanting: milkweed doesn't love being moved once the taproot develops, so transplant as early as the weather allows, ideally when nights are consistently above freezing. The younger the seedling, the better it handles transplanting.

For your scale (a few hundred plants), I'd suggest starting with Swamp milkweed (Asclepias incarnata), it's the most versatile of our species, germinates reliably, tolerates a range of soil conditions, and doesn't spread aggressively like Common milkweed can. Butterfly milkweed (Asclepias tuberosa) is also beautiful and pollinators love it, but it's a bit slower to establish.

You can find our stratified seeds here (ready to plant, no extra cold treatment needed from you): https://lasclay.com/en/products/graines-semences-asclepiade-stratifiees-froid

That would save you the stratification step entirely and get you started faster.

What you're doing on Madeline Island sounds wonderful, and it's exactly the kind of habitat those butterflies need.

Warmly,
__
 Gabriel Gouveia 
Co-founder
Lasclay.com
